title: Peer table
description: The other plans this plan names: peers.toml at the plan zone root. A peer is another project's plan repository, bound here to a local alias and identified by the plan_uid that plan declares in its own config.toml. The alias is local and means nothing outside this file; the uid is the identity and never changes; a url is a locator and is replaceable. The file is earned, not scaffolded: its absence is legal and means the plan names no peers. Nothing here is authoritative about the peer — attaching refuses a clone whose config.toml disagrees with the row it filled.

peers.description: One table per peer, keyed by the alias this plan chose for it. Two plans may both call a peer `payments` and mean different things, which is why a needs id carrying an alias resolves only through the file it was written beside.

alias.description: The local name for a peer, in the slug grammar. Unique within this file, and never equal to this plan's own project_id: without that rule a prefixed needs id has two candidate meanings. The alias is also the readable name, so a row carries no second label.

uid.description: The peer's plan_uid, as that plan declares it. This is the identity and everything else in the row is a hint. A uid appears in at most one row, and never equals this plan's own: both are cross-file facts the checker owns, because neither is visible to a schema reading one file.

urls.description: Where the peer's plan repository can be cloned, in the order attaching tries them. At least one: a peer nobody can locate is not a peer, and no value is guessed on a project's behalf.

url.description: A location carrying an explicit accepted scheme, either https or ssh. A bare account name in the userinfo is allowed because it names an account. A colon there is where a password goes, so it is refused, and the percent sign is refused with it: without that, %3A carries the same colon past the check. A committed file is read by everyone who clones this plan, so a credential in it is a leak whatever the tool prints. The url is used as written: the tool relies on no host configuration that rewrites one url into another, because a rewritten url is not the one under review.
